analysis.one_liner: Makes the new federal private-school tuition tax credit available in every state, without states' permission.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in September 2026, has no cosponsors and sits in the Senate Finance Committee with no vote scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: A 2025 tax law created a federal income tax credit, worth up to $1,700 per donation, for people who give money to organizations that hand out private K-12 school tuition scholarships. That law only turned the credit on in states that chose to allow it. This bill would strike that state opt-in requirement, so the credit would be available everywhere automatically. [S1]
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers who donate to private-school scholarship organizations — a credit works best for households with tax liability and $1,700 in spare cash — plus private schools and the scholarship organizations that would receive a new stream of federally subsidized donations in states that never opted in.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Private-school donors, schools, and scholarship funds

how_it_helps.text: Removes the requirement that a state opt in before its residents can claim the federal credit for donations to elementary and secondary school scholarship organizations. [S1]

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, who absorb the cost of the credits as reduced revenue; states also lose their authority to decide whether this private-school tuition subsidy operates within their borders, a guardrail the 2025 law put in place.

drawbacks.text: The credit is a dollar-for-dollar reduction in federal taxes for donations to private-school scholarship funds, so it directs federal revenue toward private K-12 tuition while ordinary taxpayers who cannot afford an extra $1,700 donation get nothing from it. [S1]
Striking the opt-in requirement removes the only control states had over whether the program operates within their borders, overriding state legislatures that chose not to allow it. [S1]

Money steered to private-school tuition comes on top of existing public school funding obligations, and a similar federal credit is widely understood to function like a school voucher that benefits families already in or near private schools.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrow: families who receive scholarships and donors who can claim the credit. The cost is broad — a new federal revenue loss and the elimination of states' say over a private-school tuition subsidy. The bill changes nothing else about the credit, so it does not add any income limits or accountability in exchange for removing the state gate.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent straight to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat with no cosponsors and no action since September 2026. [S3]

narrative.text: Sen. Bill Cassidy introduced the bill on September 17, 2026, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance. [S3]
No further action, markup, or vote appears in the record; Congress remains in session through January 3, 2027. [S3]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one yet: the bill has gone nowhere, so state opt-in requirements and current federal revenue remain untouched. If it died, the advantage would sit with states that declined the program and with public-school funding advocates.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, no one; the bill is stalled

for.name: Sen. Bill Cassidy
for.role: U.S. Senator from Louisiana and bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to eliminate the state opt-in requirement for the education scholarship credit. [S1]

sides.party_line_note: No votes or cosponsors exist to show which party supports or opposes it; the sponsor is a Republican and the bill sits in a Republican-controlled committee with no record of movement. [S1][S2][S3]

industries.industry: Private K-12 schools and scholarship-granting organizations
industries.note: The bill hands these organizations a new stream of federally subsidized donations in states that never opted in, making private tuition cheaper for donors' chosen schools. The cost shows up as lost federal revenue and as reduced state control over education dollars.

A dollar-for-dollar federal credit steered toward private-school tuition gives families and donors a reason to shift spending and enrollment away from public schools, whose funding follows enrollment in most states. States lose the opt-in gate that let them decline the program.

industries.industry: Higher-income households with private-school tuition bills
industries.note: A tax credit for donations is most useful to households that already have $1,700 of spare cash and tax liability, and scholarships commonly help families already in or near private schools rather than opening new options broadly.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors and only weeks left before the Congress ends on January 3, 2027, the bill is very unlikely to get a committee markup or floor vote on its own. Its only realistic path is being folded into a larger tax bill, which is a long shot; the most likely outcome is that it dies quietly when this Congress adjourns.
